chapter: Barry Martin and New Orleans tours to England
title: Kid Sheik's first tour and New Orleans musicians in England; decline of trad
summary: Martin returns, Kid Sheik is brought over in 1962-63 without work permits, followed by Kid Thomas, Emmanuel Paul and George Lewis; then the end of the trad boom, the bands' later fates, recording difficulties and brass bands.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Howard was John Handy. It's interesting in this respect because John Handy had never been heard of in England before 1961, and of course Handy's gone on to great things since then. This is partly due to Barry's efforts in England and on the continent. He came back in late 1961, early 62, duly inspired a far better drummer. He had lessons from Joe Watkins and Si Frazier, and this had changed his outlook completely. He kept the same personnel but took them off the road, and they did very few jobs while he sort of knocked them into shape with what he wanted them to do. And this is the difference. At that time, by this time it was about 1962. The Chris Barber Band had gone on to being a very professional unit. The Ken Collier Band had stayed exactly as it was, and it still is. The Humphrey Littleton Band had gone on to a more progressive style. And people at the Barry Martin Band, the smaller bands, were beginning to become known. This was just before what was known as our trad period in England. There were many, many small bands cropping up at that time. The Barry Martin Band was just about the finest of the bands around at that time. There were literally hundreds of small bands cropping up overnight all over the country, including Ackerbilt, really, which came up from the west of England. And the Terry Lightfoot Band, which were very well known in England. There were a lot of bands at this time. Well, Barry knocked his band into shape, and he decided the only way, the thing to do for the fellas in New Orleans was to start promoting as well. He played through 1962, working on a first tour. And with the help of Sammy Remington, who is well known in America, and in Europe for that matter now, he now resides in Denmark, Sammy. He has a band in Denmark. They decided to bring over Kid Sheik. It was a very amateur effort that I helped on this very first tour. We had no idea that we had to have Ministry of Labour permits, work permits, etc. What happened was, we just wrote to Sheik and asked him if he would come, and he said yes. He jumped on the boat, arrived at Liverpool, and they promptly decided to send him back. Because he had no work permit, nothing at all. A frantic phone call from the Board of Trade, in rushing about, and they decided to let him stay, providing he took it as a holiday. And he didn't work here. Well, eventually, Kid Sheik stayed here in England for about three months. He played about four nights a week with the Barry Martin Band. Another band, he played with Keith Smith, and any other band he could get work with. And he was quite happy with this arrangement. And he was the pioneer, Kid Sheik was the pioneer of real New Orleans music in England. He taught the local fellas a hell of a lot. And also promoted the Barry Martin Band. Before this, the only other band that had come to England, a New Orleans band, was in late 1959, when the George Lewis band came over. George Lewis himself came over in 1957, and played with the King Collier band. It wasn't a great success. It wasn't widely advertised, while it wasn't widely publicised. But for the few who saw George with the King Collier band, this inspired many people. The person promoting Paddy McKeeran lost a tremendous amount of money over this early tour. But Harold Davidson, who was about the largest promoter in England, decided in 1959 to have a sort of three band project. He brought over the George Lewis band, the Kid Ory band, and Earl Hines. They lost a tremendous amount of money. The whole project was shelved. And this was another one of the reasons why Barry decided that these things were done on a smaller scale. They could still be done. And after the sheep tour, it was decided between a sort of small society we set up, a small group of people in the south of England, a small group in the north of England, to try to bring over at least one or two musicians from New Orleans per year. This helped in many ways. It gave the New Orleans musicians more work, and they became widely known, especially people like John Handy. But it also promoted the Barry Martin band tremendously. Kid Cheek went back on. He was followed the following year, 1964, by Kid Thomas and Emmanuel Paul. And at the same time, late in 1964, George Lewis came to play with the Barry Martin band. It was the second to last tour of George May. The Martin band still had the same personnel, the same type of music, and still are today, for that matter. By 1964, 1965, the British sort of trad period had just about petered out. It'll all go around again in one big circle. It's pretty quiet on the traditional side at the moment, you see, since about 1964. From that time, the 6th of 1964, the bands that were left, Ken Collier has gone his own sweet way, still plays on pretty quietly, doing the same things he always has done. Humphrey Littleton now plays only progressive jazz. He has a line-up of trumpet and about three saxophones, baritone, horn, melton and soprano on occasions, and plays mainly progressive jazz for private parties. He was playing one job a week at the Six Bells at Chelsea, and they have visiting musicians, the type of Jimmy Witherspoon, and this type of singer does work with the Humphrey Littleton band. Chris Barber and Ken and Ackerbill mainly stay on the continent now. They do most of their work in Germany, and even as far as Poland, behind the own curtain. Of the smaller bands, Barry Martin band is still going strong, and the small bands such as John Casimir's band and the brass band side... Mike Casimir, who has a band and also leads the only brass band we have in England, in the Midlands, there's Dan Pawson's band, and other small ones which are quite well known to a minority, well known in their own particular area. If anything special happens, they all group together, and are known by the chosen few in England that follow this type of music. As far as recordings go in England, the smaller bands don't really get a chance. No major recording company will entertain a small British jazz band at all these days. Barry Martin records mainly for Doug Doble's 77 label, and a subsidiary label called Swift, and of course for his own labels, he runs Mono and Rhythm Records. Steve Lane's band mainly, or only record really, for their own VJM label. And this is the set up. There isn't a major company in England which will record British jazz, well not even the progressive style. Columbia, now and again, will record a modern band, but the traditional style musicians, they don't get a looking unless they they record for their own labels, or for a label which is only closely connected with local traditional music. That's really about like the whole set up with British jazz as such, other than the brass band period, which started, again, the first brass band to play was around about 1960. Kichik played in a brass band in 1961 in England. He was the first New Orleans musician to play in a brass band in England. I believe to this day is the only one to march with a British brass band. Mike Casimir is the only organised brass band at present. They're playing for carnivals, fates, and what we have as donkey derbies, and this type of thing. Very spasmodic work. They're mainly pick-up bands, they're not steady personnels at all. They play only really during the summer. They do protest marches, and C&B banner bomb marches, and this type of thing.
